reviewStatus: Original synthetic teaching examples. Independent clinical review is pending.

calibrationSource.title: University of Waterloo: ECG display calibration

patterns.name: Sinus rhythm
patterns.clue: Regular atrial activation is followed by ventricular activation. Measure the PR and QRS before judging them by appearance.
patterns.limits: This schematic illustrates an organized sinus pattern. It does not measure cardiac output or establish that every lead, coronary artery or clinical finding is normal.
patterns.prompt: Connect electrical timing with blood flow: why can an organized ECG coexist with impaired pumping?

patterns.name: Sinus bradycardia
patterns.clue: The P-to-QRS relationship is maintained while the cycle length is longer. Here 60 / 1.25 gives 48 ventricular complexes per minute.
patterns.limits: A slow sinus rate may occur with conditioning, medication effects or illness. A number alone does not establish symptoms or a need for treatment.
patterns.prompt: Compare a resting athlete with a person who has new syncope: what additional evidence changes the interpretation?

patterns.name: Sinus tachycardia
patterns.clue: P waves precede narrow complexes with a short R–R interval. The modeled rate is 60 / 0.48 = 125 per minute.
patterns.limits: The rate describes a response, not its cause. Exertion, fever, pain, reduced circulating volume and other conditions can produce a fast sinus rate.
patterns.prompt: Explain how reduced stroke volume might accompany a compensatory rise in heart rate without proving a specific diagnosis.

patterns.name: Atrial fibrillation pattern
patterns.clue: Look for the combination of irregular ventricular timing and absent organized P waves. Irregularity alone is insufficient.
patterns.limits: Artifact and other irregular rhythms can confuse a short strip. Clinical confirmation uses an interpretable recording; this example cannot choose anticoagulation or cardioversion timing.
patterns.prompt: Describe the timing evidence, then name one missing clinical fact that would matter beyond rhythm recognition.

patterns.name: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
patterns.clue: Atrial activity repeats twice as often as ventricular complexes in this model. At 2:1 conduction, some flutter activity overlaps the QRS or T wave.
patterns.limits: A ventricular rate near 150 does not alone establish flutter. Other conduction ratios and other causes of a regular fast rhythm occur.
patterns.prompt: Calculate both rates from their separate intervals and explain why they differ.

patterns.name: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia
patterns.clue: The rhythm is fast and regular with narrow QRS complexes (narrow means under 120 ms; the modeled QRS is 80 ms). Atrial activation cannot be confidently separated on this strip.
patterns.limits: The image supports a narrow-complex tachycardia pattern, not a unique re-entry mechanism. It cannot distinguish every supraventricular cause or establish clinical stability.
patterns.prompt: Separate the directly observed rate and QRS width from the unproven claim that the mechanism must be AVNRT.

patterns.name: Junctional escape pattern
patterns.clue: A slow regular rhythm has narrow ventricular complexes and no identifiable preceding P wave in this projection.
patterns.limits: This is compatible with a junctional escape rhythm; absent visible P waves alone do not prove the pacemaker location. P waves may be hidden, retrograde or visible in another lead.
patterns.prompt: Explain why a narrow QRS suggests relatively coordinated ventricular activation but does not locate every part of the conduction pathway.

patterns.name: First-degree AV block pattern
patterns.clue: Every P conducts, but the modeled PR interval is 260 ms. The delay is measured from P onset to QRS onset. Adult reference PR is 120–200 ms, so the modeled value is prolonged.
patterns.limits: A prolonged PR interval describes timing rather than the precise site or cause of delay. Medication history, previous ECGs and symptoms add context.
patterns.prompt: Contrast delayed conduction with a P wave that fails to produce a QRS.

patterns.name: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) pattern
patterns.clue: Atrial timing remains regular while the PR interval lengthens through conducted beats; a P then lacks a QRS and the sequence restarts.
patterns.limits: This illustrates a specific sequence. A single dropped QRS without its neighboring PR intervals cannot establish this pattern.
patterns.prompt: Use the P-onset and PR measurements to explain which clock stays regular and which conduction interval changes.

patterns.name: Mobitz II pattern
patterns.clue: Conducted beats retain the same PR interval, with intermittent nonconducted P waves. This example includes a wide QRS: the modeled duration is 140 ms against an adult reference of under 120 ms.
patterns.limits: The pattern warrants prompt clinical assessment because advanced conduction disease may be present. A 2:1 block alone cannot reliably be assigned Mobitz I or II from PR behavior.
patterns.prompt: Compare this 3:2 sequence with the progressively changing PR intervals in the Mobitz I example.

patterns.name: Complete AV block pattern
patterns.clue: P waves and ventricular complexes follow independent schedules. The gap from the nearest preceding P to each QRS shortens beat by beat (260 ms, then 110 ms), and the P waves at 3.34 s and 4.94 s fall inside a QRS or T wave.
patterns.limits: This model specifies absent atrioventricular conduction. AV dissociation by itself can occur in other circumstances, so rate relationships and the full recording matter.
patterns.prompt: Trace atrial and ventricular event times separately; explain why choosing the nearest P does not create a true PR relationship.

patterns.name: Premature ventricular complex pattern
patterns.rate: Sinus rhythm with one early beat
patterns.clue: A premature broad complex differs from the surrounding narrow complexes and is followed by a longer interval. The T-wave direction also differs.
patterns.limits: This constructed example is compatible with a PVC. Timing, other leads and clinical context help distinguish ventricular ectopy from an aberrantly conducted supraventricular beat.
patterns.prompt: Compare the early beat with its neighbors using onset, width, atrial relationship and the following pause.

patterns.name: Regular wide-complex tachycardia
patterns.clue: Fast, regular, broad complexes have a similar shape from beat to beat (broad means 120 ms or more; the modeled QRS is 160 ms). This is compatible with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.
patterns.limits: A single schematic cannot exclude supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy or pre-excitation. Real wide-complex tachycardia requires urgent clinical assessment; stability and pulse are not visible here.
patterns.prompt: State the observed pattern first, then the uncertainty that remains about its mechanism.

patterns.name: Torsades de pointes pattern
patterns.clue: Broad complexes vary in direction and amplitude. The supplied context includes a preceding prolonged QT, which distinguishes the intended torsades example from polymorphic VT with normal QT.
patterns.limits: The QT interval cannot be measured during this run. Under AHA 2025 guidance, sustained polymorphic VT requires immediate unsynchronized shock; magnesium may be considered for recurrence associated with long QT. A strip alone is not a resuscitation protocol.
patterns.prompt: Explain why both the changing morphology and the preceding QT context matter. Do not infer a normal pulse from organized-looking deflections.

patterns.name: Ventricular fibrillation pattern
patterns.clue: The signal lacks repeatable organized ventricular complexes. Counting the largest deflections would create a misleading heart-rate estimate.
patterns.limits: In an unresponsive patient without normal breathing or a definite pulse, VF is a shockable arrest rhythm. Artifact can resemble chaotic activity; actual assessment and resuscitation follow the relevant emergency protocol.
patterns.prompt: Explain the difference between recognizing a chaotic pattern and assessing the patient or equipment.

patterns.name: Asystole-like flat signal
patterns.clue: No organized cardiac complexes are modeled. A nearly flat recording can also result from equipment or connection problems.
patterns.limits: A flat image cannot confirm cardiac arrest by itself. Confirmed asystole in cardiac arrest is nonshockable; this example does not replace patient assessment or a resuscitation algorithm.
patterns.prompt: Name the clinical and recording checks needed before treating a flat trace as a biological finding.

patterns.name: ST-segment elevation pattern
patterns.clue: The ST segment is displaced above the baseline in this synthetic projection. Measure the displacement without turning the measurement into a diagnosis.
patterns.limits: ST elevation has ischemic and nonischemic causes. Regional distribution, other leads, symptoms and change over time matter. Troponin above an assay-specific threshold indicates injury, not myocardial infarction by itself.
patterns.prompt: Explain why this one trace cannot identify a coronary territory or establish STEMI.

sources.title: ACC: High-sensitivity troponin and chest pain evaluation

patterns.name: Prominent pointed T-wave pattern
patterns.clue: The T waves are relatively tall and pointed in this example. QRS complexes remain narrow; a complete stereotyped progression is not required for a potassium disorder.
patterns.limits: T-wave appearance neither confirms potassium concentration nor reliably excludes dangerous hyperkalaemia when absent. Sample quality, a measured potassium result and the clinical situation must be assessed together.
patterns.prompt: Contrast true hyperkalaemia with an elevated potassium caused by sample hemolysis. Explain why a reassuring-looking ECG cannot resolve that distinction.

sources.title: UK Kidney Association: Hyperkalaemia guideline, updated July 2026

patterns.name: Ventricular pre-excitation pattern
patterns.clue: A short PR is followed by a slurred initial QRS upstroke and a widened complex. The model includes an actual gradual delta-like segment. Adult reference limits: PR 120–200 ms and QRS under 120 ms; the modeled PR is 100 ms and the modeled QRS is 140 ms.
patterns.limits: A pre-excitation pattern does not by itself establish symptomatic Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome. It also cannot identify a pathway location from one projection.
patterns.prompt: Connect early ventricular activation to the altered QRS onset, and distinguish a pattern from a clinical syndrome.

patterns.name: Ventricular pacing pattern
patterns.clue: A modeled pacing stimulus precedes each broad ventricular complex. The temporal relationship is consistent with electrical capture in this example.
patterns.limits: Electrical capture is different from mechanical capture or adequate perfusion. Some modern pacing stimuli are difficult to see on surface ECGs.
patterns.prompt: Explain what evidence would be needed to connect the paced electrical event with an effective contraction.
